Philippine Senator Ronald dela Rosa has fled the Senate, where he was hiding out from arrest. ( AP Photo: Aaron Favila )

Senator Ronald dela Rosa has escaped the Philippine Senate, where he had been holed up since Monday after shots were fired in the building.

Senator dela Rosa is wanted by the International Criminal Court for alleged crimes against humanity over the country's deadly "war on drugs".

Police in the Philippines are investigating whether the shooting was instigated to help Senator dela Rosa escape.

A Philippine politician wanted by the International Criminal Court (ICC) has escaped the country's Senate building, where he had been hiding out to avoid arrest.

Senator Ronald dela Rosa's escape from the heavily guarded building came after multiple gunshots were heard on Wednesday night.

The Senate was forced into lockdown and people inside ran for cover as the shots rang out.

Police are now investigating whether the shooting was instigated to help Senator dela Rosa slip out of the Senate.

Police officers stand outside the senate building after gunshots were heard inside. ( REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez )

The 64-year-old had been under the Senate's protection and hiding out in his legislative office since Monday, when the ICC confirmed it was seeking his arrest on charges of crimes against humanity.

Senator dela Rosa was formerly the country's police chief, during which time he oversaw former Philippine president Rodrigo Duterte's deadly "war on drugs".

Authorities are still trying to work out who fired the gunshots heard inside the Senate building in the Philippines, prompting people to run for cover.

The ICC confirmed on Monday its warrant charges Senator dela Rosa with the crime against humanity of the murder of "no less than 32 persons" between July 2016 and the end of April 2018.

The shooting came hours after Senator dela Rosa had appealed on social media for his supporters to mobilise, claiming law enforcement officers were on their way to arrest him.

He has denied any wrongdoing, and filed an emergency petition with the Supreme Court in the Philippines on Wednesday urging it to block any attempt to transfer him to The Hague.

But Philippine Senate President Alan Peter Cayetano confirmed his ally had escaped the Senate, where he had been taking refuge.

“There is no obstruction of justice,” he said.

He read a text message from Senator dela Rosa's wife, Nancy, which apologised for the turmoil that his presence in the building had created.

"It's for this reason I'm sure Ronald made his escape," the message said.

The message did not disclose Senator dela Rosa's whereabouts, but said fleeing "was not part of the plan".

Military personnel in camouflage enter the Senate building on Wednesday night. ( REUTERS/Eloisa Lopez )

Police spokesperson Randulf Tuano said investigations were underway to determine who was behind the shooting, with bullet casings and assault rifle magazines recovered.

He said one person had been detained, and had "provided names" that were being verified.

National Bureau of Investigation chief Melvin Matibag said the possibility that the incident was staged was also part of the probe.

Political analyst Richard Heydarian told ABC's The World Senator dela Rosa's arrest should have been imminent.

"Right now we're getting conflicting messages whether there was a shooting between a supposedly unidentified group of people … or whether there actually was a failed apprehension or arrest operation," he said.

"Trust is very low, and there's a lot of suspicion.

"People are wondering whether that was just a fig leaf or a cover to allow Senator dela Rosa to escape."

Military personnel in camouflage enter the Senate building on Wednesday.

Mr Heydarian said many are demanding the Senate face legal ramifications for their role in blocking Senator dela Rosa's arrest.

"The Senate, or the leadership of the Senate, has been in obstruction of justice," he said.

"In fact, some are saying maybe the leadership of the Senate should face legal ramifications for blocking the enforcement of this valid arrest.

"This is precisely why the ICC is coming in, because there's a concern, as long as he is in the Philippines, [that] he's going to be protected."

Protesters had been gathering outside the Senate prior to the shooting, demanding the arrest of Senator dela Rosa.

Among them were the parents of people killed in the country's "war on drugs".

Llore Pasco, the mother of two men killed in the anti-drug campaign, said the spectacle of a powerful politician being granted due process and political protection stood in sharp contrast to the fate of her sons.

"That's how it is. If you are rich and powerful, even if you are at fault, you are still protected," the 71-year-old said.

"Surrender and face the crimes you're accused of, if you really have no guilt.

"There is a process, that's what you call due process."

Police personnel stand behind their shields outside the Senate in Manila. ( AP Photo: Gerard Carreon )

Dahlia Cuartero, whose son was killed in 2019, said the ICC had given her and other victims a voice they never had in the Philippines.

"Justice in this country is really only for the rich. For us poor people, we have nothing to rely on," she said.

Vice President Sara Duterte is in The Hague visiting her father, and likened Mr dela Rosa's case to what she called her father's "illegal abduction".

"What we are seeing now is the administration using all government resources to demolish political opposition," she said, in comments shared by her office.

She is also facing her own impeachment trial in the Senate on separate matters.

UK Health Secretary Wes Streeting has resigned from the government, in what his allies say is preparation for a challenge to Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer.

Sir Keir is attempting to weather a string of ministerial resignations and scores of MPs' demands that he set out a timetable for his exit, after voters handed Labour a catastrophic result at local elections last week.

To make it onto the ballot in a leadership contest, any potential challenger must have the backing of 81 of the party's 403 MPs — a number already surpassed by those who have publicly called on the PM to quit.

UK cabinet minister Wes Streeting has quit his role as health secretary, piling pressure on under-fire prime minister Sir Keir Starmer to stand down.

Sir Keir, who won a landslide election less than two years ago, is facing growing calls to quit following catastrophic local election results last week which saw the Labour Party lose almost 1,500 local council seats to its opponents.

Mr Streeting is widely viewed as a potential leadership candidate, and his allies say he is preparing a tilt for the top job.

UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer is under enormous pressure from within his party to quit. ( Reuters: Toby Melville )

"It is now clear that you will not lead the Labour Party into the next general election and that Labour MPs and Labour Unions want the debate about what comes next to be a battle of ideas, not of personalities or petty factionalism," Mr Streeting said in a letter to the prime minister published on X.

He went on: "You have shown courage and statesmanship on the world stage — not least in keeping Britain out of the war in Iran.

Another likely challenger, former deputy prime minister Angela Rayner, said on Thursday that she had reached an agreement with tax authorities to clear up questions about her taxes that forced her to leave the cabinet last September.

While Mr Streeting comes from the moderate wing of the centre-left Labour Party, as does Sir Keir, Ms Rayner is a favourite of more left-wing voters, calling on the party to do more to boost the minimum wage and raise taxes on the rich.

Ms Rayner told the Guardian newspaper that Sir Keir should "reflect on" his position, adding that she was ready to "play my part" in any leadership election if Mr Streeting were to trigger a contest.

Former deputy prime minister Angela Rayner could launch her own bid for the Labour leadership. ( Reuters: Chris J Ratcliffe )

Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham is also widely seen as a potential candidate, though he would have to find a way back into parliament before he could run.

Mr Burnham cancelled his regular Thursday appearance on a local BBC radio program this week to "prioritise discussions arising from last week's elections."

Allies have suggested a sitting member of the House of Commons could resign to make way for Mr Burnham to run in a special election.

Sir Keir, who won an overwhelming majority in the 2024 general election, is attempting to weather a string of ministerial resignations and scores of MPs' demands that he set out a timetable for his exit.

Sir Keir Starmer is striking a defiant tone, despite a growing number of his Labour colleagues urging him to step down.

A large majority of voters are frustrated with his government, which has failed to deliver on pledges to boost economic growth and improve living standards for working people, in part due to stubbornly high consumer price inflation.

He has told allies that he will fight a leadership challenge should a rival stand against him, warning colleagues that any leadership contest would plunge the government into "chaos" at a time it should be focused on issues like the cost-of-living crisis and the war in the Middle East.

Under Labour Party rules, any potential challenger to the prime minister would have to have the backing of 81 of the party's 403 MPs to make it onto the ballot.

More than that number have publicly called on Sir Keir to quit in recent days.

By Paul Johnson

Thu 14 May 2026 at 9:48pm

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor has denied permanent residents who are not Australian citizens will be targeted under any potential future Coalition government.

During his budget in reply speech on Thursday night, Mr Taylor singled out that group.

"We will remove Labor's handouts for non-citizens," Mr Taylor told parliament.

"Many Australians would be surprised to learn that non-citizens are eligible for welfare.

"We've already announced that the first homebuyer 5 per cent deposit scheme will be reserved for Australian citizens only. That's because Labor has allowed some 50,000 non-citizens to access this scheme."

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers the day after delivering the Federal Budget. ( ABC News: Matt Roberts )

Mr Taylor told 7.30 his focus was on putting Australian citizens first, rather than targeting immigrants.

"I think it's extraordinary at at a time like this that the government has cut support for older Australians' private health insurance and yet there is welfare for Anglo-Australian citizens."

"Citizenship is a privilege and it's something we want people to get something from.

"If you contribute to this country, we want to contribute back and that's what citizenship is all about but when someone can get all the benefits without that, it becomes meaningless."

Mr Taylor added that some non citizens have access to what he said were "17 different" welfare programs.

People from Chinese and Indian diasporas — often have to give up their citizenship to become Australians.

Asked for his message to those people, Mr Taylor denied they would be made to give up anything.

"We're not forcing anyone to give up anything," Mr Taylor told 7.30.

"We're saying if you want access to the privileges which we believe should be privileges of citizenship, you need to become a citizen.

"You need to make a choice.

"The idea someone should arrive and the moment they arrive here get access to family tax benefit for instance, I think for Australians that's just not on at a time like this when we're really struggling."

Asked if that might affect the number of skilled migrants wanting to come to Australia, Mr Taylor said he did not believe that was the case.

One Nation has long spoken about lowering immigration numbers. ( ABC News: Ian Cutmore )

"There's always a long queue of people wanting to come to this country," he told 7.30.

"I believe it's the greatest country on Earth.

"If people come to this country in order to to receive welfare in the first couple of years of being here, perhaps that's not an appropriate circumstance.

"it's appropriate that people come spend some time and become a citizen. That's how most countries in the world work."

While Mr Taylor said that Australians are struggling, so is the Coalition.

One Nation has been on the rise and Barnaby Joyce has been revelling in the party winning the Farrer by-election. ( AAP: Bianca De Marchi )

For the first time in history the Coalition lost former leader Sussan Ley's seat of Farrer in a by-election that saw One Nation's David Farley claim the party's first ever lower house seat in federal parliament .

Asked how big the threat was from One Nation, Mr Taylor said his budget in reply speech was not about stopping any momentum One Nation has.

However, also appearing on 7.30 former Nationals leader Barnaby Joyce said the Coalition had copied from the One Nation playbook.

"I'd like to thank them for basically reading off the One Nation script," Mr Joyce said before commenting on skilled migration.

"As we know we've been bringing in about the population of Canberra a year. It sort of waned a little bit lately, but we just didn't have the houses, we didn't have the schools.

"We certainly didn't have the dams, we didn't have the universities, we didn't have the hospitals."

Asked if he thought Mr Taylor's speech would stop the flow of Australian voters towards One Nation, Mr Joyce had a simple answer.

"No."
